Hook: In his autobiography, the mathematician Richard Bellman recalled the autumn of 1950, when he went to work at the RAND Corporation, which did research for the United States Air Force. His first task was to find a name for his mathematics of decisions made in stages. The Secretary of Defense, he wrote, had a pathological fear and hatred of the word research, and the Air Force answered to him. So Bellman chose programming, in the sense of planning, as in a military schedule, and dynamic, because the problems change over time and because, he said, it is impossible to use the word dynamic as an insult. It was, he wrote, something not even a Congressman could object to. His memory of the date has been questioned, since the Secretary he named took office only in 1953; the name stuck either way.

Seventy years on, dynamic programming is how economists solve economies that have no formula. Guess the value of being in each situation, apply Bellman's equation, and repeat. Each round the guess improves, and after 333 rounds the growth model of Part twenty-nine has settled, in a few hundredths of a second on a laptop. Inside an estimation, a model like this is solved again for every set of parameters the estimator tries, thousands of times. So speed matters; and so does a harder question.

The question: how is an economy that has no formula solved, and how do you know the answer is right? Why does repeating Bellman's equation converge at all? Which methods are fast, and which are accurate? How do you know a computed answer is right? And what breaks when the model grows?
Economics, Built. Part fifty-one: computing economies.

This part opens Act ten, the graduate core: the tools that turn the models of the course into research. The Bellman operator, why it converges, and value and policy iteration. Grids, interpolation, and a method with no root finding at all. Projection and perturbation, and when certainty equivalence misleads. Accuracy, measured; expectations; and continuous time. Then constraints that bind, the curse of dimensionality, and how to make a computation that someone else can repeat.
Operator: Chapter one. The Bellman operator as a contraction.

Write the growth model as Bellman did. The value of starting a year with capital k is the best, over next year's capital, of this year's utility plus the discounted value of next year. Read the right-hand side as a machine. Put in a guess V, a value for every capital stock; the machine, the Bellman operator T, returns a new guess. The answer is the value function the machine leaves unchanged: a fixed point, V equals T of V. The model is the one of Part twenty-nine: utility with an elasticity of substitution of a half, a capital share of 0.36, eight percent depreciation, and a discount factor of 0.96.

Why should repeating the machine settle anywhere? Draw a machine on a line, a cartoon of T. The dashed diagonal is where the answer equals the guess. The purple line is the machine: it maps each guess to an answer, and it is flatter than the diagonal, so it brings any two guesses closer together. That is a contraction. Start anywhere, apply it, apply it again: the steps walk in to the one point where the line meets the diagonal. Stefan Banach proved in 1922 that a contraction on a complete space has exactly one fixed point, and that iterating from any start reaches it. The Bellman operator is such a machine, on the space of value functions.

On the real model, measure it. Each round, record how far the new value function is from the old, at the worst capital stock, on a log scale. After a few rounds the points fall on a straight line, and its slope is the discount factor: each round the change shrinks by a factor of 0.960, exactly the 0.96 the theory promises. That also says how long it will take: to shrink the change a million times needs about three hundred and thirty-eight rounds, and it took 333. Patience is expensive: with a discount factor of 0.99, as in quarterly models, it would take four times as many.

How do we know the Bellman operator is a contraction without proving it from scratch each time? David Blackwell gave two conditions in 1965 that are easy to check. Monotonicity: if one guess of the future is everywhere better than another, the operator's answers keep that order. A better future never makes today worse. Discounting: add the same amount to every future value, and today's value rises by only beta times that amount. Both are checked here on random guesses: the order is kept, and the discounting holds to the last digits a computer carries. Together they make T a contraction with modulus beta, so the value function exists, is unique, and iteration finds it. The rest of this part is about doing that fast, and accurately.
Iteration: Chapter two. Value and policy iteration, timed.

Value iteration has a weakness the last chapter exposed: it crawls. Each round the values improve by only the factor beta, so with a patient household they creep towards the answer, 333 rounds here. But look at the decisions instead of the values. After round 74, the best choice of next year's capital at every grid point never changes again. More than three quarters of the work only polishes numbers whose decisions are already right. That suggests a better plan.

Ronald Howard's policy iteration, from 1960, works on the decisions. Take a policy, and work out the value of following it forever, not one round at a time but exactly, in one step. Then improve the policy with a single Bellman step, and stop when no choice changes. The bars count the grid points whose choice changed in each round: all three hundred at first, then fewer and fewer, then none. 18 rounds instead of 333, and the same policy at every grid point. Even with each round doing more work, it is about 2 times as fast here, and the gain grows with patience, because value iteration slows as beta approaches one and policy iteration barely notices.

Why is it so much faster? Fix a policy sigma. Its value satisfies a linear equation: this year's utility under the policy, plus beta times the value wherever the policy sends you. The matrix P sigma records where that is, so each row has a single one in it, and the system has just two entries a row. A computer solves such a sparse system in one step, and that one step does the work of hundreds of rounds of value iteration. In fact policy iteration is Newton's method applied to the Bellman equation, which is why it converges in a handful of rounds where value iteration needs hundreds.
PlayIt: Chapter three. Play it: which grid is fine enough?

Your turn. Value iteration chooses next year's capital from a grid of points. On a grid of thirty points the policy is a staircase; on a hundred, a finer staircase; on a thousand, it is hard to tell from the accurate rule. You must report the economy's steady-state capital, where the policy crosses the diagonal, to within one percent. Which grid will do: thirty points, a hundred, a thousand, or none of them? Pause, and choose.

Here are the steady states each grid implies, as a share of the true one. Thirty points: 8.6 percent too low. A hundred: 2.5 percent too low, still outside the band. A thousand: 0.25 percent, inside it. Only the finest grid will do. Notice the direction: on a grid the household can only choose among a few capital stocks, and the rounding does not cancel out; it drags the steady state down.

A better yardstick than any one number is the Euler-equation error, which chapter eight builds properly. For now: at each capital stock, how far is the rule from satisfying the household's own first-order condition, as a fraction of consumption? With thirty points the worst mistake is about one dollar in 6 of consumption. With a hundred, one in 23. With a thousand, one in 246. Ten times the points buys about ten times the accuracy, and costs a hundred times the work, because each point must compare itself with every other. Fine enough depends on the question; the habit to learn is to measure the error rather than guess it.
Interpolation: Chapter four. Between the grid points.

The staircase of the last chapter came from a restriction: next year's capital had to be one of the grid points. The best of seven points may be some way from the true best. Instead, keep the value function only at the grid points, fill in between them by interpolation, and search the filled-in curve for its peak, wherever it lies. A golden-section search does that without derivatives: each step keeps the better sixty-two percent of the interval, so sixty steps pin the peak down to far less than a billionth of the range.

How much does it buy? For reference, the thousand-point grid, faint. Forty points with straight lines between them nearly match it, at about one dollar in 122. The same forty points joined by a cubic spline: one in 1.1 million, thousands of times better, because the value function is smooth and a spline uses its curvature. And twelve points, placed where Chebyshev says and joined by one polynomial: one dollar in 4.7 million. Smooth problems reward smooth approximations.

Why Chebyshev's points? Carl Runge found the warning in 1901. Take this smooth, harmless-looking bump. Pass one polynomial through eleven evenly spaced points on it, and the polynomial swings wildly near the ends, missing by 1.9; adding more evenly spaced points makes the swings larger, not smaller. Put the eleven points where Chebyshev's nodes are, crowded towards the ends, and the error falls to 0.11, and keeps falling as points are added. Where you put the points matters as much as how many you use.

Three ways to place twenty-four points. Evenly, the natural first choice. Chebyshev's nodes, crowded at both ends, the right choice for a single polynomial across the whole range. And a grid that crowds its points near the borrowing limit, the one the household of chapter five uses, because that is where its consumption rule bends sharply. The rule is simple to state and easy to forget: put the points where the function bends.
Egm: Chapter five. The endogenous grid method.

The household of Part twenty-two: it earns an income that moves persistently up and down, saves at a fixed return, and cannot borrow. Its assets next year are this year's, with interest, plus income, minus consumption, and must not fall below zero. Its rule is the Euler equation: the marginal utility of consuming today equals beta times R times the expected marginal utility tomorrow, unless the borrowing limit binds. The usual way to solve it: at every level of assets, search for the consumption that makes the equation hold, a root to find at every grid point, in every one of hundreds of rounds.

Christopher Carroll's trick, published in 2006, turns the problem around. Put the grid on next year's assets instead of this year's. Then the right-hand side of the Euler equation, which depends only on next year, is known from last round's consumption rule. Inverting marginal utility gives today's consumption directly: no search, just a power. The budget then says what assets today lead to that choice: a equals c plus a prime minus y, over R. Those assets fall wherever they fall, so the rule is interpolated back onto the grid; below the first of them the borrowing limit binds, and the household consumes everything it has. Today's grid is found, not chosen, which is where the name comes from.

Here are the rules it finds, for the lowest, middle and highest of five income levels. With the lowest income and little wealth, the household consumes everything it has: the rule lies on the dashed line, because the borrowing limit binds. With more wealth it starts to save, and the rule bends away. Higher income lifts the whole rule, by less than the income, because some of a good year is saved for bad ones.

How much faster is it? Plot each method by the time it takes and the worst error it leaves, both on log scales, so lower and further left is better. Value iteration on grids of a hundred to eight hundred points: each doubling of the grid costs four times the time and buys only a little accuracy. The endogenous grid method, with two hundred points, sits far below and to the left. Against value iteration with 800 points it is 85 times as fast and 43 times as accurate. Extending the blue line, value iteration would need a grid more than a hundred times finer to match it, and more memory than a laptop has.
Projection: Chapter six. Projection: the rule as a polynomial.

A different idea, from Kenneth Judd in 1992: stop storing the rule at grid points, and write it as a formula. Approximate consumption by a sum of Chebyshev polynomials with unknown coefficients theta. For any theta, the Euler equation leaves a residual: how far marginal utility today is from its discounted value tomorrow. Choose the n coefficients so that the residual is exactly zero at n points, Chebyshev's nodes: that is collocation, n equations in n unknowns, solved by Newton's method. Or make the residual zero on average against each polynomial: that is Galerkin's method. Either way, the whole policy becomes a handful of numbers.

Here is the residual of a polynomial of degree three, four coefficients, across the range of capital. It wiggles, as it must, because a cubic cannot be exactly the true rule. But it passes through zero at the four nodes where collocation forced it to, and between them it stays small. Chebyshev's nodes are spread so that those wiggles are about as even, and as small, as any placement can make them.

And as the degree rises? The worst Euler error falls steadily, from about one dollar in two hundred and fifty with a straight line, to one in 6 million at degree eight, each extra degree making the rule about 4 times more accurate. This is what mathematicians call spectral convergence, and it is the reward for a smooth problem. Galerkin's method, at degree four, lands in the same place as collocation. And the whole computation takes a few thousandths of a second. Projection's weakness is the other side of the same coin: a kink, such as a borrowing limit, ruins a single smooth polynomial, which is why the household used a grid.
Perturbation: Chapter seven. Perturbation, and when certainty equivalence misleads.

The third family of methods works from a single point. Write next year's capital as a Taylor series around the steady state. The first coefficient comes from differentiating the Euler equation once at the steady state, which gives a quadratic; the stable root is 0.924, so the gap to the steady state closes by about 7.6 percent a year, the speed of convergence of Part twenty. The second coefficient comes from differentiating twice, and the equation for it is linear. This is perturbation, the workhorse of central banks' models: fast, and exact at the point it starts from.

How far can the series be trusted? Measure each approximation's mistake in next year's capital, against the accurate rule, across a wide range. At the steady state both are exact. The first-order rule, a straight line, drifts away as capital moves far from the steady state; the second-order rule bends with the truth and stays closer for longer. Within the range an economy usually visits, both are good; measured by Euler errors, first order is right to about one part in two hundred, second order to about one in eight hundred. Far from home, after a war or in a deep crisis, a local method can mislead.

Now the deeper trap. A first-order approximation of a model with uncertainty has a property called certainty equivalence: the rule depends on the average of future shocks, never on their size. Solve the household twice. Once with its income known for certain, at the same average; once with the income uncertain, as it is. The uncertain household consumes less at every level of wealth: at assets of two, 0.22 less, about a fifth of a year's income, saved against bad years. This is precautionary saving, the buffer stock of Part twenty-two. A first-order perturbation cannot see the gap at all; a second-order one sees part of it, as a constant shift. When risk itself drives behaviour, as with saving, asset prices or default, a method must see the risk.
Continuous: Now let time run continuously. A household earns one of two incomes, switching between them at random, and saves or borrows at a fixed rate, down to a limit. Its Bellman equation becomes the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation: the return on being in a state equals the flow of utility, plus the value of the wealth it is accumulating, plus the expected gain from a switch of income. Because time is continuous, the best consumption satisfies a plain first-order condition, marginal utility equals the slope of the value function, with no search. Yves Achdou, Jiequn Han, Jean-Michel Lasry, Pierre-Louis Lions and Benjamin Moll showed in 2022 how fast this can be solved.

How is it solved? On a grid of wealth, the slope of the value function is a difference between neighbouring points. The trick is to take the difference in the direction the household is moving: forward where it saves, backward where it runs its wealth down. This upwind rule is what keeps the method stable. Then each step solves one linear system for the whole value function at once, an implicit step that can be as large as you like. The system has 1,000 unknowns, but each grid point talks only to its two neighbours and to the same wealth in the other income state, so of a million entries only about three thousand are not zero. 9 steps, a few hundredths of a second.

The results. Saving: with low income the household runs its wealth down, faster the more it has, until it reaches the borrowing limit and stops there; with high income it saves, less as it grows richer. And the distribution of wealth across many such households, which in discrete time needs a separate simulation. Here it comes from the same sparse matrix, transposed: the Kolmogorov forward equation. 3.6 percent of households sit exactly at the borrowing limit, low earners who have run out. That spike is a feature of the economics, and the method captures it exactly.
Bounds: Many economic constraints bind only sometimes. The household's borrowing limit is one: with little wealth and low income, it would like to borrow and cannot, so it spends everything. With a little more wealth it starts to save, and its rule follows the Euler equation. Where one regime gives way to the other, the rule has a kink. A single smooth polynomial cannot bend that sharply and smears the corner, which is why this household was solved on a grid. The endogenous grid method finds the kink exactly: it is the first point of the endogenous grid, below which the limit binds.

The zero bound on interest rates, from Part thirty, is the other famous case. Take the New Keynesian economy of that part, and let the natural rate of interest fall to minus two percent for a year. A linear solution that ignores the bound has the central bank cut its rate to about minus 3.6 percent, and the output gap falls to about minus 1.7 percent. But the rate cannot go below zero. Luca Guerrieri and Matteo Iacoviello's method guesses which quarters the bound binds in, solves the linear model for that sequence, checks whether the rule would ask for a negative rate anywhere else, and repeats. Here it settles after 2 guesses, with the rate at zero for 3 quarters. Respecting the bound, the output gap falls to minus 3.4 percent, twice as deep. The constraint that binds only sometimes is exactly the one that decides how bad the recession is.

What to take away. Kinks break the smooth methods: a polynomial or a Taylor series assumes the rule is smooth everywhere. Grids and regime methods cope: the endogenous grid finds the kink, and guess and verify finds the regime. The safest way solves the whole nonlinear model with the constraint inside it, at a higher cost. And whichever is used, the errors must be checked on both sides of the kink and at the corner itself, where approximations are worst.
Dimension: Chapter twelve. The curse of dimensionality.

Every method so far had a state with one or two parts: capital, or assets and income. Real models have more. With five grid points in one direction, a grid has five points. Add productivity, and it has twenty-five. Add two more parts and it has six hundred and twenty-five. With ten parts, nearly ten million, and that with only five points in each direction, far too coarse to be accurate. Bellman named the problem himself in 1957: the curse of dimensionality.

The way out begins with a Russian mathematician, Sergey Smolyak, in 1963. A full grid takes every combination of points in every direction, so its size multiplies with each new part: on a log scale, a straight line up. Smolyak's sparse grid keeps only the combinations that matter most for smooth functions: many points along each axis, few where several directions vary at once. Its size grows like the square of the number of parts, not exponentially. With twenty parts: 841 points, against about a hundred trillion. Dirk Krueger and Felix Kubler brought the method into economics in 2004.

Does the sparse grid give up accuracy? Test it on a smooth function of four variables, whose value is known everywhere. The full grid's error falls as points are added. Smolyak's falls too, and for a given accuracy it uses fewer points: in four dimensions, roughly a half or a third as many. In ten or twenty dimensions, where the full grid cannot even be stored, the saving is what makes the problem possible at all. The price is smoothness: a kink or a strong interaction between the variables erodes the advantage. Beyond a few dozen dimensions, even sparse grids give out, and the frontier uses neural networks as the approximation, the subject of Part sixty-four.
Dials: Chapter fourteen. The Dials: parameters against method error.

Every solver in this part was fed numbers: a discount factor, a capital share, and an elasticity of intertemporal substitution of a half. The last is one of the Dials, from Part seven. Robert Hall found it near zero in aggregate data; surveys of hypothetical choices, about 0.2; Annette Vissing-Jorgensen, about a third for stockholders and nearly one for bondholders; Jonathan Gruber, from tax variation, about two; Tomas Havranek's meta-analysis, near zero in macro data and about a third in micro data; and asset-pricing models assume one and a half. Contested, across a factor of ten or more.

Now set the two kinds of uncertainty side by side, on a log scale. Take consumption when capital is eighty percent of its steady state. Change the elasticity of substitution from the film's half to one, and consumption changes by 3 percent; to a quarter, by 2 percent the other way. A good method's error is about a hundred thousand times smaller: lost entirely in the uncertainty about the parameter. But a careless one, the thirty-point grid of chapter three, gets the steady state wrong by 9 percent, as large as the whole dispute about the parameter. So a method need not be perfect, only good enough that its error is small beside what we do not know about the economy; and only measuring shows which side of that line it is on.
Practice: Chapter fifteen. In practice: model teams and estimation.

Who uses these methods? Central banks keep model teams; the Federal Reserve's large model, FRB/US, has been in use since 1996. Many of their smaller models are solved by perturbation, often with Dynare, free software developed since the 1990s. Academic economists estimate models structurally, which means solving the model again inside every evaluation of the likelihood. Models with many different households, the subject of the next part, solve a household like chapter five's for every candidate interest rate. And firms use the same dynamic programming to price seats and rooms, manage inventories and replace equipment.

Why speed matters so much there. An estimation guesses the parameters, solves the model, computes what the model says about the data, compares, and guesses again, thousands of times over. John Rust's nested fixed point of Part forty-four works exactly so, solving the bus engine problem inside each step. A solver a thousand times too slow makes the estimation a thousand times too slow, and a solver that is not accurate makes the estimates wrong.

Called it? A forecast about the machines themselves. In April 1965 Gordon Moore, then director of research at Fairchild Semiconductor, plotted a handful of points and predicted in the magazine Electronics that by 1975 the cheapest chips would carry about sixty-five thousand components, the number doubling every year. In 1975 he reported that the projection had been met, and revised the pace to a doubling every two years. That pace held for half a century: the largest microprocessor grew from about two thousand three hundred transistors in 1971 to 58 billion in 2021, doubling about every 2.0 years. The verdict: right, with one revision, and the revision was made in the open. Every method in this part rides on that curve.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: solvers that differentiate.

The frontier first. Estimation needs to know how the solution moves when a parameter moves. The collocation equations hold at the solution for every value of beta, so they can be differentiated: the derivative of the coefficients is one linear solve with the matrix Newton's method already built. Here, how consumption at the steady-state capital responds to the discount factor: minus 5.7558, the same, to six digits, as solving the model twice and differencing. Differentiable programming, the machinery of modern machine learning, does this automatically through any solver, so that estimation can follow gradients instead of guessing.

Second, the curse of dimensionality, attacked with machine learning. Draw states of the economy at random, with no grid at all. Let a neural network propose the policy at each. Compute the Euler residuals there, the yardstick of chapter eight, and adjust the network's weights to shrink them. Lilia Maliar, Serguei Maliar and Pablo Winant, and Marlon Azinovic, Luca Gaegauf and Simon Scheidegger, published such methods in 2021 and 2022. They solve economies with hundreds of state variables, such as many overlapping generations, and they must be checked the same way as any other method: by Euler errors on states the network never saw.

What remains open? Certifying accuracy: in a hundred dimensions the errors can only be sampled, and a bound on the worst one is hard to come by. Solving models with millions of different households quickly, for which the newest methods linearize around a solved household in sequence space, the subject of the next part. Knowing in advance when a local method is safe and when only a global one will do. And making computations that involve random training as reproducible as the ones in this film.
